extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, and academic authors (scholarly publishing community)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and discussion of the practices, purposes, and decision-criteria used by journals to perform an initial editorial (desk) review and to reject or pass papers to external peer review. Covers who makes decisions, why papers are filtered early, and trade-offs between quality, fit, novelty, and business considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial editorial review for quality, relevance, and scientific interest
rubrics_metrics.description: An important step that precedes external peer-review in nearly every journal — initial editorial review for quality, relevance, and scientific interest (associative quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually performed by in-house editors; can lead to the rejection of a high number of submissions without external peer-review. Helps cope with high submission volumes and spare reviewers from obvious mismatches. Practices vary by journal; often involves at least two editors agreeing a paper should be bounced out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit to journal / journal identity (scope/brand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a submission is 'right for you' — matches the journal's identity, place, scope, and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If editors lack a clear journal identity they cannot market the journal or target readers. Fit is a common ground for editorial rejection (e.g., wrong journal). Editors use brand-associated traits to quickly identify misfits; poor fit may prompt an offer to transfer to a more appropriate sister journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological and scientific quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the paper is flawed, poorly done, or of insufficient scientific quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flawed or poor studies are legitimate grounds for editorial rejection. This is distinct from importance; methodological problems justify desk rejection and avoid wasting reviewers' time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / general interest / citation potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of how important or broadly interesting the results are — often framed as 'of general interest' or judged by likely citation impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many editorial rejections are motivated by perceived lack of significance or low citation potential; some editors explicitly estimate expected citations when deciding. This criterion is debated because 'importance' can be subjective or luck-driven; journals sometimes reject for low perceived significance but offer transfer to lower-tier journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the work presents novel or groundbreaking ideas/results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel work can be treated inconsistently: editors may reject genuinely new work out of unfamiliarity, or conversely chase flashy novelty to boost impact. For controversial or highly novel claims, editors and reviewers expect especially strong evidence and rigorous methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and required submission materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of required disclosures, supplementary data, complex datasets, online summaries, image sets, and other materials expected by the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incomplete or improperly prepared submissions create extra staff and editorial burden and may be filtered out. The growing complexity of publication requirements is a factor in increasing use of editorial screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious mismatch / low probability of surviving peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors filter out manuscripts they judge will not survive external peer review (obvious misfits or 'dreck').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a pragmatic filter used to reduce reviewer burden and provide faster decisions to authors. It is widely practiced to spare reviewers and focus resources on manuscripts with a realistic chance of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and timeliness of decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing a quick decision (including prompt rejections) is a priority for authors and an explicit function of editorial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors generally prefer immediate or fast rejections rather than undergoing months of review that results in rejection. Editors can supply brief statements explaining a desk rejection to help authors find an appropriate venue sooner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who should decide: professional editors vs practicing-scientist editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether desk-rejection decisions should be made by full-time professional editors or by practicing scientists (peer editors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for practicing scientists emphasize scientific judgment and maintaining 'the integrity of Science'; arguments for professional editors emphasize generalist perspective, dedicated time, and editorial experience. Many journals use combinations or oversight to balance strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision process: multiple-editor agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Most editorial review processes involve at least two editors agreeing a paper should be rejected without external review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement for multiple editors to concur varies across journals; having more than one editor involved is a common procedural standard to reduce subjectivity and error in desk rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for reviewer workload and volunteer status
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial screening is used to avoid imposing on overstretched volunteer reviewers by sending them manuscripts that are poor fits or obviously unpublishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors use desk rejections to be fair to reviewers and to allocate peer-review resources efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer/cascade options to other journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections for lack of general interest are often accompanied by an offer to transfer the manuscript to a lower-rated or sister journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects journals' business models and helps authors place work faster; it also illustrates that editorial rejection may be about fit/impact rather than pure quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial and market considerations (especially for books)
rubrics_metrics.description: For scholarly books, acquisitions decisions hinge not only on scholarly fit but also on sales potential and marketability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book publishers often reject on grounds of insufficient expected sales even if scholarly quality is acceptable; this differs from article-based journal decision criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation of single-review rejections (reviewer credibility check)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a manuscript is rejected on the basis of a single damning review, the editor may check the reviewer's publishing and reviewing history before finalizing the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural safeguard ensures that a one-off negative report by an unreliable reviewer does not inappropriately eliminate a manuscript; the page cites Physica Scripta checking reviewer credentials in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial staffing and resourcing as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may hire staff specifically to provide an initial filter because of high submission volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial review allows staff to focus on manuscripts with chance of publication and to manage workload; staffing levels and publisher profit motives influence how aggressive initial screening is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associative quality (brand effects on perceived quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality is associative: perceptions of the journal or community influence how individual papers are evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Branding and the journal's position in the ecosystem affect editorial decision-making; this associative quality can speed identification of misfits but may also bias decisions toward conformity with perceived journal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mega-journal vs traditional journal editorial filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: Mega-journals tend to omit rigorous associative editorial review and emphasize a broad methodological filter, while traditional journals apply stronger editorial selection based on fit/importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mega-journals publish more papers and rely less on brand-based filtering; this affects media coverage and focus compared with journals that practice strong initial editorial rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary-claim standard (controversial work must be especially convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that challenges current thinking or is highly controversial must be methodologically sound and present especially convincing evidence (e.g., larger studies, better statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors of controversial claims are advised to present extraordinary evidence, perhaps by incremental publication steps (e.g., starting with a review or by submitting to venues that emphasize methodological soundness like PLoS ONE if appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explanatory feedback when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When conducting desk rejections, editors can provide a brief statement explaining why the manuscript was rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief explanations help authors find a proper home more quickly and are considered valuable by authors; some journals also offer an option to dispute and request full peer review, with an explicit warning about the likely time cost.
